messages.author: 1c29719a737f20c6
messages.subject: Is MCMC Obsolete?
parts:
I'm just entering the exciting world of INLA (and Bayesian spatial analysis in general); the possibilities seem limitless!  I hope to post some other questions as soon as I'm able to formulate them properly, but for right now, my question is this:  does the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation make Monte Carlo methods (e.g., Markov Chain Monte Carlo, MCMC) obsolete?  

If the INLA approximation does just as well as sampling from the posterior distribution, and does it much faster, why would anyone ever use MCMC?  Put another way, is there really a free lunch?  I guess the answer to this question hinges on how accurate the approximation is.  One paper (Carroll, R., et al. 2015. "Comparing INLA to OpenBUGS for hierarchial Poisson modeling in disease mapping," Spatial and Spatiotemporal Epidemiology, 0: 45-54) conducted a simulation study and concluded that R-INLA's default settings did not recover the true parameters as accurately as BUGS, but that after fine-tuning the parameters, R-INLA performed comparably to BUGS.  Is anyone aware of other studies like this?  Thoughts?    

Many thanks to Håvard Rue, his team, and his students for developing R-INLA and providing such helpful online tools for learning and using it!  

Regards,
David Crow, 
California Department of Public Health

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Is MCMC Obsolete?
parts:
There are room for both, both MCMC and INLA, and one does not rule out
the other. For latent Gaussian models (LGMs), then there is so much
structure that can be made use of, and this is what INLA does. So you
can see it as a special approximation/solution for a restricted set of
models, whereas MCMC is a generic approach for 'all' models.

If MCMC is ``needed'' for those models INLA can do well, that is
another issue, yes.

H
